label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article II, Section 3. The President gives Congress information of the state of the Union and recommends measures to it; on extraordinary occasions he may convene both houses or either of them, and if they disagree about the time of adjournment he may adjourn them to such time as he thinks proper; he receives ambassadors and other public ministers, takes care that the laws be faithfully executed, and commissions all the officers of the United States.
This story is about who may cut firms off from money systems.

In 1794, the joint resolution of March 26, 1794 provided "that the President of the United States be authorized to give such instructions to the revenue officers of the United States, as shall appear best adapted for carrying the said resolution into full effect."

In 1807, the Act of December 22, 1807 provided "that the President be authorized to give such instructions to the officers of the revenue, and of the navy and revenue cutters of the United States, as shall appear best adapted for carrying the same into full effect."
The US Treasury said it put sanctions on eight money firms in Canada.
The strongest argument against this is that the executive must carry out laws on foreign dealings, so it may cut firms off once a law covers that field.
We read this clause to mean the executive carries out the laws, not invents the financial sanctions.
We read this clause to mean Congress lays the embargo first; only then may the executive put it into effect.
This keeps the trade power with the people's branch.
